title: "I have stopped. You stop."
hook: he runs and cannot catch the Buddha, who walks slowly; the sword drops (MN 86)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Angulimala: three warnings, and the Buddha walked on down the forest road. Your line was walk on. What did you step toward? Day seventy-two.

Legs pumping, lungs burning, and no closer than before. It's the shape of a bad dream, and it's where we left Angulimala. Sword and shield, bow and quiver, running flat out after one monk walking at an ordinary pace down a forest road. And the sutta says he could not catch him. He ran with all his strength. The monk walked calmly. And the gap didn't close. Finally, out of breath, the killer of the forest road stops and shouts.
screen: `WHERE WE LEFT ANGULIMALA.` → `RUNNING, AND THE GAP WON'T CLOSE.` → `HE STOPS AND SHOUTS.`

segments.voice: He shouts: stop, monk! And the Buddha, still walking, answers: I have stopped, Angulimala. You stop too. Angulimala is baffled, and a little offended. You monks are supposed to speak the truth. You're walking, and you say you've stopped. I'm standing still, and you tell me to stop. What do you mean? And the Buddha answers him in a verse. In paraphrase: I have stopped for good. I've laid down violence toward every living being. You are the one who hasn't. You're the one still running. That's the whole turn of the story, in one line. The texts are clear that the chase itself was a wonder, a monk walking and a runner who can't catch him. But the real miracle isn't about feet. Stopping, here, means stopping harm. The Buddha's body is moving, and he's perfectly still, because he has laid down the thing that drives people to hurt. Angulimala's body is standing still, and inside he's still running, still chasing, still armed. Something in the verse lands. Angulimala throws his sword and his weapons over the edge of a ravine, into a chasm. He bows at the Buddha's feet and asks to go forth. And the Buddha says the old, simple words of ordination: come, monk. That's all. The man with the finger garland walks back up the road as a monk, beside the one he'd been chasing. When King Pasenadi rides out soon after with hundreds of horsemen to hunt the killer down, he finds a quiet monk sitting in the monastery. The king is stunned. What he couldn't tame with punishment or weapons had been tamed without either.
screen: `STOP, MONK!` · `I HAVE STOPPED. YOU STOP TOO.` · `STOPPING MEANS LAYING DOWN HARM.` · `THE WEAPONS GO INTO THE RAVINE.` · then, large: `I HAVE STOPPED.`

segments.voice: Settle and breathe. Think of one small way you keep running at yourself or someone else. A sharp tone. A late-night scroll that leaves you worse. A story you keep telling about someone. Picture it as a weapon in your hands. Feel its weight. Then, on an out-breath, picture setting it down. Just for today. Notice how your body feels without it. The bell holds the time.
Thito. Stopped, standing still: the Buddha's answer to Angulimala, that real stopping isn't about the body. It's laying down harm.
Your line: I have stopped. Today, when you catch yourself about to repeat the habit, say it quietly: I have stopped. Day seventy-two.

screen: `DAY 72 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE MONK WHO WAS STONED.`

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers quote 'I have stopped, you stop too' when they retell the Angulimala story, and use it to show that stopping, in the teaching, means laying down harm.

fork.setup: you're Angulimala. the monk has just said: I have stopped for good. I've laid down violence toward every being. you're the one still running. what do you do?
options: throw your weapons into the ravine and ask to go forth.
walk away back into the forest.
fork.reveal: he hurls his weapons into a chasm, bows, and asks to go forth. 'come, monk,' the Buddha says, and that is his ordination.

original.note: Pali: I have stopped, I am standing still. The first words of the Buddha's answer.

trapdoor: what you thought: a monk winning a footrace with a trick.
what it means: a killer running and a monk walking, and the monk is the still one, because he has laid down harm.
what a scholar hears: MN 86: thito aham, Angulimala, tvañ ca tittha; 'ehi bhikkhu', come, monk: ordination by the Buddha's own word.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): hook no longer opens 'You know the dream...'; cut the superlatives 'the most feared man in the kingdom' and 'the earliest, simplest form of ordination' (trapdoor), and the 'often'/'common theme' claims in howItsDone. Removed the 'Here's the practice:' opener.
The Buddha's verse is paraphrased; no public-domain English translation of MN 86 is quoted.
The chase described as a feat of psychic power in the sutta (iddhabhisankhara); the script says 'a wonder'. Confirm.
Pasenadi with 500 horsemen: in MN 86 the king comes to the Buddha at Jeta's Grove and meets Angulimala there; the script says 'sitting in the monastery'. Confirm.
